title.en: Explain the U-shape of LRAC through returns to scale

say.en: Over a few years a firm can build a bigger factory or move to a smaller one. Then no cost is fixed, and the size of the firm decides its average cost. In this lesson: Define LRAC and LRMC.
Explain the U-shape of LRAC through returns to scale.
Relate LRMC and LRAC.

body.en: In the long run all inputs are variable, so there are no fixed costs: total cost and total variable cost are the same. *Long-run average* cost $LRAC = TC/q$ and long-run marginal cost $LRMC = \Delta TC/\Delta q$. The LRAC curve is U-shaped: it falls while the firm enjoys increasing returns to scale, is flat over constant returns, and rises when decreasing returns set in.

points.en: No fixed cost in the long run

narration.en: In the long run there are no fixed costs. The long-run average cost curve is U-shaped because of returns to scale.

body.en: Like short-run curves, LRMC is U-shaped. When LRMC is below LRAC, LRAC falls; when LRMC is above LRAC, LRAC rises; LRMC cuts LRAC from below at its minimum point. Because of increasing returns to scale, larger firms in many industries (steel, cement, power) can produce at a lower average cost.

problem.en: A firm spends ₹1,000 to produce 100 units. In the long run it doubles all inputs; total cost rises to ₹2,000 and output to 300 units. Find LRAC before and after and name the returns to scale.

steps.en: Inputs doubled, output tripled: increasing returns to scale, so LRAC falls.

answer.en: LRAC falls from ₹10 to about ₹6.67: increasing returns to scale.

narration.en: Let us work this out together. A firm spends ₹1,000 to produce 100 units. In the long run it doubles all inputs; total cost rises to ₹2,000 and output to 300 units. Find LRAC before and after and name the returns to scale.

say.en: Let us work this out together. A firm spends 1,000 rupees to produce 100 units. In the long run it doubles all inputs; total cost rises to 2,000 rupees and output to 300 units. Find LRAC before and after and name the returns to scale.
LRAC before equals 1000 over 100 equals 10 rupees.
LRAC after equals 2000 over 300 is approximately 6.67 rupees.
Inputs doubled, output tripled: increasing returns to scale, so LRAC falls.
So the answer is LRAC falls from 10 rupees to about 6.67 rupees: increasing returns to scale.
